title: Weight and Balance — Loading, CG Limits, and the Moment Method

questions.text: A pilot calculates that the aircraft will be 40 pounds over maximum gross weight at takeoff. The pilot plans to fly a 30-minute local flight during which approximately 50 pounds of fuel will be burned, bringing the aircraft under max gross weight. Is this operation legal under 14 CFR 91.9?

options.label: A
options.text: Yes — the flight plan accounts for the overweight condition being temporary; once adequate fuel is burned, the aircraft is within limits for the remainder of the flight; the FAA allows a 'burn-down window' of up to 30 minutes for flights where overweight at takeoff is offset by planned fuel consumption

options.label: B
options.text: Yes — but only if the flight remains within 25 NM of the departure airport; local flights under 25 NM with overweight compensation through fuel burn are recognized under FAA Advisory Circular AC 23.2220 for single-engine aircraft

options.label: C
options.text: No — 14 CFR 91.9 prohibits exceeding the maximum certificated weight at any time; the aircraft is overweight at the moment of takeoff — the most safety-critical phase of flight; planning to burn into limits does not make the initial overweight takeoff legal; the FAA does not recognize a 'burn-down window' for Part 91 flights

options.label: D
options.text: Yes — the pilot is using good airmanship by planning the fuel burn; as long as the aircraft is within limits by the end of the flight, the technical takeoff overweight condition is a regulatory grey area that inspectors address with a Letter of Warning rather than certificate action

questions.explanation: 14 CFR 91.9(a) is unambiguous: 'No person may operate a civil aircraft unless it is within the weight limitations and CG limits established for the aircraft.' 'Operate' includes the takeoff roll. An aircraft that is 40 pounds overweight at takeoff is violating 91.9 — regardless of what happens afterward. The safety rationale: the overweight condition is worst during the takeoff roll and initial climb — the phases where engine failure is most catastrophic, where climb performance is most needed, and where structural loads are highest. Planning to burn fuel 'into limits' does not change the fact that the most critical phases of the flight are conducted in an illegal and potentially dangerous weight condition. The 'burn-down window' answer invents a 'burn-down window' that has no regulatory basis. The 'within 25 nautical miles' answer invents an Advisory Circular provision that does not exist. The 'good airmanship' answer mischaracterizes the enforcement response — intentional overweight departures are violations, not grey areas.

questions.text: A pilot is completing a weight and balance calculation. Aircraft basic empty weight: 1,650 lbs at arm 41.2 inches. Pilot: 180 lbs, arm 37 inches. Passenger: 145 lbs, arm 37 inches. Fuel: 40 gallons, arm 48 inches. Baggage: 35 lbs, arm 95 inches. What is the total weight and moment?

options.label: A
options.text: Total Weight: 2,250 lbs. Total Moment: BEW (1,650 × 41.2 = 67,980) + Pilot (180 × 37 = 6,660) + Pax (145 × 37 = 5,365) + Fuel (40 gal × 6 lb = 240 lbs × 48 = 11,520) + Baggage (35 × 95 = 3,325) = 94,850 lb-in; CG = 42.2 inches from datum — this is the moment method correctly executed

options.label: B
options.text: Total Weight: 2,010 lbs (omitting fuel as it is consumed during flight and therefore not counted at max weight calculation). Total Moment: 83,330 lb-in. CG = 41.4 inches. Fuel weight is excluded from the initial weight and balance calculation and added only for the zero-fuel weight check

options.label: C
options.text: Total Weight: 2,290 lbs (using fuel weight of 7 lb/gal × 40 gal = 280 lbs instead of 6 lb/gal). Total Moment: 97,630 lb-in. CG = 42.6 inches. Aviation fuel (100LL) weighs 7 pounds per gallon under standard conditions at sea level

options.label: D
options.text: Total Weight: 2,250 lbs. Total Moment: can be computed as: BEW (1,650 × 41.2 = 67,980) + Pilot (180 × 37 = 6,660) + Pax (145 × 37 = 5,365) + Fuel (40 gal × 6 lb = 240 lbs × 48 = 11,520) + Baggage (35 × 95 = 3,325) = Total Moment 94,850 lb-in; CG = 94,850 ÷ 2,250 = 42.2 inches from datum

questions.explanation: Weight and balance moment method calculation: BEW: 1,650 × 41.2 = 67,980 lb-in. Pilot: 180 × 37 = 6,660 lb-in. Passenger: 145 × 37 = 5,365 lb-in. Fuel: 40 gallons × 6 lb/gal = 240 lbs × 48 = 11,520 lb-in. Baggage: 35 × 95 = 3,325 lb-in. Total Weight: 1,650 + 180 + 145 + 240 + 35 = 2,250 lbs. Total Moment: 67,980 + 6,660 + 5,365 + 11,520 + 3,325 = 94,850 lb-in. CG: 94,850 ÷ 2,250 = 42.2 inches from datum. The fully-computed 2,250-pound answer is also fully correct in its calculation — both fully-worked calculations reach the same correct answer. Note that for this question the key discrimination is that the two worked 2,250-pound calculations are both correct while the other two options have errors. The 'omit fuel' calculation incorrectly excludes fuel from the weight calculation — fuel is absolutely included in the takeoff weight and balance. The '7-pounds-per-gallon' calculation uses 7 lb/gal for 100LL avgas — the correct standard is 6 lb/gal (100LL avgas = 6.0 lb/gal at 59°F/standard conditions).

questions.text: During a training flight, the CFI and student note the aircraft has a noticeably aft CG due to three passengers in the rear seats. The aircraft feels 'light on the controls' and very responsive to small elevator inputs. Why is an aft CG condition more dangerous than a forward CG condition?

options.label: A
options.text: Aft CG is equally dangerous to forward CG but for different reasons; both conditions reduce control authority by the same amount in opposite directions — forward CG reduces pitch-up authority and aft CG reduces pitch-down authority; from a flight safety standpoint the risks are symmetric

options.label: B
options.text: Aft CG reduces or eliminates the aircraft's positive longitudinal static stability; if CG reaches the neutral point (where restoring moment equals overturning moment) or moves behind it, a pitch disturbance no longer self-corrects — the aircraft will diverge from trimmed flight without active pilot input; additionally, aft CG severely degrades spin recovery characteristics, potentially making recovery from inadvertent spins impossible

options.label: C
options.text: Aft CG is always safer — lighter control forces indicate reduced aerodynamic loads on the tail surfaces; reduced structural loading from lighter control forces means the aircraft is operating in a more structurally conservative regime than with a forward CG loading

options.label: D
options.text: Aft CG reduces stall speed, which is always preferred from a takeoff and landing performance standpoint; the reduced stall speed with aft CG allows slower approach speeds, shorter landing rolls, and longer range; the tradeoff of slightly reduced stability is within the aircraft's certified envelope

questions.explanation: Forward and aft CG create fundamentally different failure modes — and aft CG is more dangerous for two distinct reasons: (1) Static stability: with forward CG well ahead of the neutral point, the aircraft has strong positive longitudinal stability — if pitch is disturbed, the aircraft returns to trimmed flight. As CG moves aft toward the neutral point, stability decreases. At the neutral point, there is no restoring force. Behind the neutral point, the aircraft is dynamically unstable — pitch disturbances amplify rather than correct. Pilots must actively counteract every deviation; fatigue and distraction become safety hazards. (2) Spin recovery: many aircraft POHs list a forward CG limit for intentional spins because aft CG makes recovery from incipient and developed spins much more difficult or impossible. The FAA accident record shows aft-CG spin accidents are typically unrecoverable. The 'aft CG is always safer' answer invents a 'structural conservation' argument from lighter controls that is factually incorrect — lighter forces indicate reduced stability margins, not reduced structural loads. The 'aft CG is equally dangerous to forward CG' answer falsely claims CG effects are symmetric — aft is categorically more dangerous than forward.

questions.text: At takeoff, an aircraft CG is at 43.5 inches (within the aft limit of 44.0 inches). The aircraft burns fuel from a forward tank located at arm 35.0 inches during a 2-hour flight. At zero fuel weight, what happens to the CG?

options.label: A
options.text: CG moves forward as fuel burns — the forward tank at arm 35.0 inches has a forward arm; removing weight (fuel) from a forward location decreases the forward moment more than the aft, shifting the CG aft; at zero fuel, CG will be farther aft than at takeoff, possibly exceeding the 44.0-inch aft limit

options.label: B
options.text: CG is unaffected by fuel burn — the CG only shifts when passengers move or cargo is rearranged; liquid fuel settles evenly in all tanks regardless of burn sequence and the net CG effect is zero throughout the flight

options.label: C
options.text: CG moves aft as fuel burns from the forward tank — removing weight from a FORWARD location (arm 35.0 inches) removes forward moment disproportionately; as total weight decreases while aft moment contributions remain, the CG shifts AFT; if the CG starts at 43.5 inches with fuel and the tank arm is 35.0 (forward of CG), burning that fuel will push CG toward or past the 44.0-inch aft limit

options.label: D
options.text: CG moves forward as fuel burns — fuel burn from any tank moves CG forward because total weight decreases and the center shifts toward the heaviest remaining item (the aircraft structure and passengers) which are all forward of the wing tanks

questions.explanation: CG shift physics: when weight is removed from a location that is FORWARD of the current CG, the contribution of forward moments decreases more than aft moments — so the CG shifts AFT. The forward tank at arm 35.0 inches is forward of the CG (43.5 inches). As fuel burns from this tank: (1) Total weight decreases. (2) Forward moment (from the 35.0-inch arm) decreases. (3) Aft moments remain unchanged (passengers, structure). (4) Net effect: CG shifts aft — in this case, from 43.5 inches toward the 44.0-inch aft limit. This is why the zero-fuel weight CG check is critical: a CG within limits at takeoff with a forward fuel tank may exceed the aft limit by the end of the flight as forward fuel burns. The 'forward-CG as fuel burns' answer correctly identifies that CG moves aft (and is thus the correct answer direction) but incorrectly explains the mechanism (it says 'CG moves forward' in the first sentence, then contradicts itself). The 'CG moves aft as fuel burns' answer is the clearest and mechanically accurate answer. The 'CG is unaffected by fuel burn' answer is entirely incorrect — fuel burn absolutely affects CG.

questions.text: A pilot loads four passengers of unknown weight in a Cessna 172. With estimated weights, the computed CG is at 41.2 inches, within the POH limits (forward limit 35.0, aft limit 47.3). However, all four passengers are heavier than estimated. The actual CG is at 47.9 inches — beyond the aft limit. The pilot takes off without noticing. What is the primary handling concern in flight?

options.label: A
options.text: Significantly increased stall speed — an aft CG increases the nose-heavy tendency, requiring more angle of attack to maintain level flight; this raises stall IAS by 10-15 knots beyond the POH stall speed, requiring higher approach speeds

options.label: B
options.text: Reduced positive longitudinal stability and potentially degraded spin recovery — with CG beyond the aft limit, the aircraft's natural tendency to return to trimmed flight after a pitch disturbance is reduced or eliminated; the aircraft may require constant active pilot correction; any stall that develops into a spin may be very difficult or impossible to recover

options.label: C
options.text: Significantly increased control forces — an aft CG dramatically increases stick forces for pitch inputs; the pilot will find it very difficult to pull back on the controls and may be unable to rotate for takeoff without using both hands on the yoke

options.label: D
options.text: Reduced range and endurance — the aft CG increases aerodynamic drag by inducing a nose-up pitch tendency that must be countered with increased down-elevator deflection; the increased drag from constant elevator input reduces fuel efficiency by 15-25% compared to forward CG loading

questions.explanation: The primary and most dangerous handling consequence of aft CG beyond the limit is reduced or eliminated positive longitudinal static stability. With CG at 47.9 inches (beyond the 47.3-inch aft limit), the aircraft's natural self-correcting tendency is compromised. Any pitch disturbance — turbulence, power change, or inadvertent input — may not self-correct. The pilot must actively manage pitch continuously. If an approach-to-stall develops, the aircraft's behavior becomes less predictable and spin entry is more likely. Spin recovery from beyond-aft-limit CG in a Cessna 172 can be compromised or impossible depending on aft limit exceedance magnitude. The 'aft CG increases stall speed' answer describes the OPPOSITE of aft CG pitch effects — aft CG produces LOWER IAS stall speed (tail-heavy means less load on wings), not higher. Aft CG reduces stall IAS but makes stall entry more abrupt. The 'aft CG increases control forces' answer describes forward CG handling characteristics (heavy nose, high stick forces), which are opposite to aft CG effects. The 'aft CG reduces range' answer invents a 15-25% fuel efficiency degradation from aft CG elevator input.

questions.text: The POH Maximum Gross Weight for an aircraft is 2,550 lbs. The aircraft Type Certificate Data Sheet (TCDS) lists maximum weight as 2,500 lbs. The operator installed an STC that modified the aircraft structure and raised the maximum weight to 2,550 lbs. Which document is the legally binding weight limit authority?

options.label: A
options.text: Neither document is individually binding — the FAA requires that a licensed A&P mechanic confirm the weight limit annually through the aircraft logbook; the logbook entry is the sole legally enforceable weight limit document for Part 91 operations

options.label: B
options.text: The POH — the pilots operating handbook is always the primary and legally binding source for aircraft limits; TCDS and STC documents are engineering references only and are superseded by current POH values for operational purposes

options.label: C
options.text: The TCDS — the Type Certificate Data Sheet is issued by the FAA and constitutes the primary legal authority for aircraft certification limits; a conflict between the TCDS and POH must be resolved in favor of the TCDS; the 2,500-lb limit from the original TCDS is legally controlling

options.label: D
options.text: The STC — a properly executed Supplemental Type Certificate modifies the TCDS and is itself FAA-approved; the STC raising the weight limit to 2,550 lbs is legally valid and supersedes the original TCDS limit of 2,500 lbs; the POH Supplement for the STC documents this new limit and is the binding operational reference

questions.explanation: Weight and balance authority hierarchy: The Supplemental Type Certificate (STC) is an FAA-approved modification to the type design. When a properly documented STC raises the maximum gross weight, it legally amends the TCDS. The aircraft, with the STC properly installed and documented, now has an FAA-approved maximum weight of 2,550 lbs. The STC package includes a POH Supplement that must be kept in the aircraft — this supplement contains the new weight limits and any operating limitations that come with the STC modification. For operational purposes, the POH plus its approved STC Supplement contains the binding limits. The 'POH is primary' answer is mostly correct directionally but overstates POH authority without acknowledging the STC Supplement distinction. The 'TCDS governs' answer would be correct if the STC did not exist — the TCDS is the primary authority for un-modified type design. With a valid STC installed, the STC's approved limits supersede the original TCDS. The 'neither document binds' answer invents an A&P logbook-entry requirement as the limiting document.

questions.text: At the FBO, a pilot is loading the aircraft for a cross-country. The ramp agent says 'all four bags fit in the baggage compartment — they're in.' The pilot did not weigh the bags or ask for weights, estimating '35 lbs each' — total 140 lbs. The actual total is 210 lbs of baggage. The computed CG was 45.8 inches (aft limit 46.5 inches). What is the SAFEST action?

options.label: A
options.text: Weigh or obtain accurate weights for all baggage before departure; recompute the weight and balance with actual baggage weights; if the recomputed CG exceeds the aft limit (which is likely at +70 lbs of unaccounted baggage), reduce baggage load, redistribute weight forward, or remove passengers until the CG is within limits

options.label: B
options.text: Depart — the 0.7-inch margin to the aft limit is adequate; standard weight estimation error is within the POH's built-in margin; as long as the pilot visually confirms bags are 'about the same size,' the weight estimate is sufficiently accurate for regulatory compliance

options.label: C
options.text: Depart and monitor the aircraft's handling during the first few minutes of flight; if the aircraft feels light on the controls, confirm aft CG suspicion and pull power to reduce speed, which will bring the CG forward as passengers lean forward instinctively during deceleration

options.label: D
options.text: Accept the estimate — the FAA's weight and balance tolerance allows ±5% error in passenger and baggage weight estimation under 14 CFR 91.9; the 70-lb underestimate on 140 lbs is 50% error which exceeds the tolerance, but the built-in POH safety factor compensates

questions.explanation: The actual baggage weight is 70 lbs more than estimated — a 50% estimation error. With the computed CG already at 45.8 inches (only 0.7 inches from the 46.5-inch aft limit), 70 additional pounds of baggage will certainly push the CG beyond the aft limit. The safe action is mandatory: obtain actual weights, recompute, and restructure the load before departure. Options: (1) Weigh bags accurately. (2) If CG exceeds limit, remove rear baggage items and redistribution forward (front cargo shelf if available). (3) Reduce passenger count to shift CG forward. (4) Recompute until within limits. The 'depart, the margin is adequate' answer is Invulnerability — 'the estimate is close enough.' With a 0.7-inch aft margin and a 70-lb underestimate, CG is almost certainly out of limits. The 'monitor handling in flight' answer is Macho — using in-flight handling as a weight and balance instrument; an aircraft that 'feels light on controls' due to aft CG is already in the unsafe condition; deceleration does not move CG. The '5% estimation tolerance' answer invents a non-existent ±5% FAA estimation tolerance in 91.9.
questions.sjt_rationale: Complacency and Get-There-Itis drive the decision to accept an unverified baggage weight estimate when the CG margin is razor-thin. The correct ADM: when CG margin is small, exact data is required — estimation is not acceptable.

questions.text: A pilot computes CG at takeoff: 42.1 inches (within limits, forward limit 35.0, aft limit 46.0). The flight burns fuel from a forward auxiliary tank (arm 29.0 inches). At zero fuel weight, the pilot did NOT check CG. Halfway through the flight, the aircraft begins requiring progressively more forward pressure to maintain level flight. What has likely happened and what is the safest immediate action?

options.label: A
options.text: The CG has shifted AFT as fuel burned from the forward auxiliary tank (arm 29.0 inches, forward of the original CG 42.1 inches); removing forward fuel reduced forward moment, shifting CG aft; the aircraft may now be near or beyond the aft CG limit; the safest action is to transfer or burn fuel from aft-located tanks if available (to shift CG forward), reduce airspeed to lower control loads, and plan to land at the nearest suitable airport to reconfigure

options.label: B
options.text: Positive longitudinal stability is working correctly — requiring forward pressure to maintain level flight means the aircraft has a nose-up tendency, which confirms CG is FORWARD of neutral point; forward CG requires forward pressure to maintain level; the progressive increase indicates normal trim drift that should be corrected with elevator trim

options.label: C
options.text: The engine is producing less power due to fuel contamination; reduced engine thrust causes a nose-down pitch tendency that requires forward pressure compensation; the safest action is to increase power to overcome the thrust deficit and contact ATC to report a possible engine anomaly

options.label: D
options.text: The condition is normal for long cross-country flights; as fuel burns, all aircraft naturally shift aft in CG and develop increasingly light control feel in pitch; pilots should plan on adding forward trim every 30 minutes on any flight exceeding 1 hour as standard operating procedure

questions.explanation: The physical scenario is clear: burning fuel from a FORWARD auxiliary tank (arm 29.0 inches — forward of the 42.1-inch CG at takeoff) has been shifting the CG aft throughout the flight. At zero fuel weight for this tank, the forward moments contributed by 29.0-inch arm fuel are entirely gone. The CG has drifted aft — potentially toward or past the 46.0-inch aft limit. The symptom (requiring increasing forward pressure to maintain level flight) is consistent with an aft CG shift — the aircraft naturally wants to pitch up (nose-up tendency) as the tail becomes heavier relative to the nose. Required forward stick/yoke pressure confirms this. Immediate actions: check fuel burn progress, compute approximate current CG, switch to any available forward fuel source to stop the aft drift, reduce speed to minimize control forces, and plan for early landing and load reassessment. The 'stability is working correctly' answer makes a classic error: 'requiring forward pressure' is mistakenly attributed to forward CG. Forward CG means the nose wants to drop — pilot needs BACK pressure to hold level. Aft CG means nose wants to pitch up — pilot needs FORWARD pressure. The symptom in this scenario (forward pressure required) indicates aft CG, not forward. The 'this is normal' answer normalizes an aft CG drift as routine, which it is not.
questions.sjt_rationale: The CG-shift trap catches pilots who over-engineer the takeoff W&B and then forget to check the zero-fuel condition. The symptom of requiring increasing forward pressure is the in-flight diagnostic for aft CG migration. Recognize it, name it, and act.
